title: A delayed tropical temperature term did not give clear added CO2 growth skill in 2012-2024
abstract: We tested whether a negative delayed tropical temperature relation adds information beyond current temperature in annual atmospheric CO2 growth. We fitted fixed models in 1966-2011 and tested 2012-2024 using the exact external inputs of an earlier campaign study. A joint model with current temperature and the mean of one-year and two-year delayed temperature reduced squared error by 2.1% beyond current temperature. The paired three-year block 95% interval was -10.6% to 11.4%. The term helped in 4 of 13 years and increased mean absolute error. All seven main sensitivity estimates were positive, but all intervals included zero. A model with no delayed temperature response gave a training lag-correlation range of -0.402 to 0.045; the observed value was -0.266. A finite-filter proof shows that a recent-mean anomaly filter can create negative lag correlations with no delayed response. These results do not establish a useful added delayed effect or prove its absence. Limits include 13 later years, revised data, annual sampling, an adapted filter, and no separation of emissions and sinks. This is a retrospective conditional test, not an operational forecast or an exact replication of the original monthly analysis. Code, aggregate evidence, source hashes, an independent arithmetic check and a byte-identical full replay are included. External source data and record-level derivatives remain outside the package.

display.caption: Added delayed-temperature skill in later years and conditional delayed coefficients. All skill intervals include zero.
The negative training statistics fall inside a fitted memoryless null range. This is a specific control and does not prove absence of carbon memory.
